weeks.objective: Read and compose numbers through one million and explain adjacent place values.

days: Day 1: Build a seven-column place-value chart.

explanation: A place-value chart has ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, hundred-thousands, and millions. Each column represents ten of the unit to its right. In 44,000 the left 4 counts four ten-thousands, or 40,000; the other 4 counts four thousands, or 4,000. The digit is the same but its value is ten times as great.

Write a number by putting each count in its own column. Empty columns need zero placeholders. For example, six hundred-thousands, three thousands, and two tens make 603,020. Expanded form shows the nonzero place-value parts, 600,000 + 3,000 + 20. Reading the thousands group first helps keep these places distinct.

Moving a digit one place left multiplies its value by ten; moving one place right divides its value by ten. This describes value, not adding ten to the number. Ten groups of 700 make 7,000, whereas adding ten to 700 makes 710. Use named units to explain which change happened.

explanation: When two numbers have the same number of digits, compare from the greatest place. Equal digits represent equal amounts, so move to the next column. The first differing column decides the order because all smaller columns together cannot outweigh one unit in that column.

The symbols < and > open toward the greater number. In 318,500 < 381,050, both numbers have three hundred-thousands but one has only one ten-thousand while the other has eight. Zeros still hold places: 407,009 has fewer thousands than 470,009 even though the same nonzero digits appear.

Ordering three or more numbers means making a chain of comparisons. Keep the original numbers intact and check each neighboring pair. A number line gives another representation: numbers farther right are greater. If a missing digit can take several values, report all values that satisfy the comparison rather than only one example.

Day 5: Explain why a rounded count may fail a capacity decision.
explanation: Rounding chooses a nearby multiple of a named place. For the nearest thousand, first locate the consecutive thousands on either side of the number. Their midpoint separates numbers that are closer to the lower thousand from numbers closer to the upper thousand. At an exact midpoint, this course rounds to the greater multiple.

The rounding place matters. A number can round to different values at the nearest ten, hundred, and thousand. Record which place you used and keep the unrounded number available. Rounding does not change the exact count; it changes the precision used to describe it.

An estimate can help check a calculation but does not replace exact counting when a limit is strict. A rounded attendance of 400 may come from 351 or 449 when rounding to the nearest hundred. Do not conclude that exactly 400 chairs will be enough from that estimate alone.

explanation: Align digits by place value so ones are added to ones and thousands to thousands. Start at the ones column. Whenever a column totals ten or more of its unit, exchange ten for one unit in the next column. Writing a small carried digit records that exchange; it is part of the next column total.

For 2,786 + 4,657, thirteen ones become one ten and three ones. The tens total includes the exchanged ten. A written algorithm is a compact record of these regroupings, not a separate kind of mathematics. Expanded sums or counting on can verify the same result.

Use an estimate to notice a result that is much too large or small, then use subtraction for an exact check. A misplaced digit can change an addend by a factor of ten. In a story, first decide whether the quantities really combine and use the same unit before adding.

explanation: Subtraction finds what remains or the distance between two quantities. Align the places and start with ones. If a column has too few units, exchange one unit from the next available place for ten of the needed unit. The whole number keeps the same value even though its representation changes.

Across zeros, exchange in stages. In 6,002, exchange one thousand to make ten hundreds; exchange one of those hundreds to make ten tens; then exchange one ten to make ten ones. The representation becomes five thousands, nine hundreds, nine tens, and twelve ones. Each exchange preserves 6,002.

Do not subtract the smaller digit from the larger digit in each column independently. That ignores which number is being subtracted. Add the difference to the subtrahend to check the result. For nearby numbers, counting upward from the smaller number can be easier than several exchanges.

explanation: Factors are whole numbers that multiply to make a given number. List pairs systematically, beginning with 1. For 36, test 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6: the successful pairs are 1 × 36, 2 × 18, 3 × 12, 4 × 9, and 6 × 6. Once the pair members meet or cross, further pairs repeat.

A prime number has exactly two positive factors, 1 and itself. A composite number has more than two. The number 1 has just one positive factor, so it is neither prime nor composite. A rectangular array with both dimensions greater than 1 demonstrates that a number is composite.

Multiples are totals made by repeated groups of a number. Twelve is a multiple of 3 because 3 × 4 = 12; 3 is a factor of 12. Do not reverse these terms. To decide whether a number is a multiple, look for a whole-number quotient or an exact multiplication equation.

days: Day 1: Generate terms from explicit starts and rules.

Day 3: Notice parity and ones-digit features.

explanation: A pattern rule tells how to create each term, and a starting value tells where to begin. Starting at 4 and adding 3 gives 4, 7, 10, 13, 16. The rule says add 3, but the terms also alternate even and odd. Explain that extra feature: adding an odd number changes parity each time.

For a shape pattern, describe the construction precisely so someone can continue it without a picture. A row of joined squares made from sticks starts with four sticks; each additional square shares one side and adds three sticks. The totals are 4, 7, 10, 13. Distinguish the count of squares from the count of sticks.

An observed feature is a conjecture until there is a reason it continues. A few terms can suggest repeating ones digits or constant differences. Link the feature to the rule, and test a competing claim with a counterexample. Different rules can match a short list, so do not pretend that a finite list forces one rule without other information.

days: Day 1: Identify the whole and equal partitions.
Day 2: Refine shaded strips and count new parts.
Day 3: Connect models to multiplication of both terms.
Day 4: Challenge claims using different-sized wholes.
Day 5: Explain one equivalence with a complete model.
explanation: A fraction names a count of equal-sized parts of one whole. The denominator names how many equal parts make that whole, and the numerator counts selected parts. To compare or rename an amount, hold the whole fixed. Half of a small sheet need not have the same area as half of a larger sheet.

If every third of a strip is split into two equal pieces, the whole now has six equal parts. Two shaded thirds become four shaded sixths. Both the selected count and the total count double, so 2/3 = 4/6. The shaded length has not grown; only the partition has changed.

Multiply numerator and denominator by the same positive whole number to describe this refinement. Multiplying only the numerator adds selected pieces without making the pieces smaller, changing the amount. A strip, area model, or number-line location should support the equation rather than merely decorating it.

days: Day 1: Regroup fine partitions into larger equal units.

Day 5: Explain why adding the same number to both terms fails.
explanation: Equivalent fractions can be made with larger or smaller counts. To rename 6/8 as fourths, group each two eighths into one fourth. Six selected eighths make three selected groups, and eight eighths make four groups in the whole. Dividing both counts by two gives 3/4.

Use a common factor to group numerator and denominator evenly. A fraction is in simplest form when no whole number greater than one divides both counts. Simplest form is useful but not more accurate than another equivalent form. The fraction 50/100 and the fraction 1/2 identify the same point.

A missing numerator or denominator can be found by tracing the factor from one known count to another. Apply the same factor to its partner. Adding the same number to numerator and denominator generally fails, because it does not preserve the size and number of groups in balance.

days: Day 1: Place fractions around half on a line.
Day 2: Use opposite sides of a benchmark to compare.
Day 3: Compare missing pieces near one.
Day 4: Identify when a benchmark is insufficient.
Day 5: Defend a contextual comparison with a fixed whole.
explanation: A benchmark is a familiar point that helps locate other numbers. For a fraction between 0 and 1, compare its numerator with half of its denominator. Three eighths is below one-half because half of eight pieces would be four pieces. Five eighths is above one-half.

If one fraction is below one-half and another is above, their order is settled without finding common denominators. Fractions near one can be compared by the missing part when appropriate: 7/8 is missing 1/8, while 5/6 is missing 1/6. Since an eighth is smaller than a sixth, 7/8 is closer to one and greater.

Benchmarks sometimes tell only part of the story. Both 2/3 and 3/4 exceed one-half, so that observation alone does not order them. Use a strip, equivalent units, or another justified comparison. Every comparison here assumes the same whole; a larger fraction of a smaller whole need not be a larger physical amount.

explanation: Three eighths means three copies of 1/8. It can be decomposed as 1/8 + 1/8 + 1/8 or as 2/8 + 1/8. Adding like-denominator fractions counts more pieces of the same size. Thus 2/8 + 3/8 = 5/8, just as two apples plus three apples is five apples.

The denominator stays fixed because the unit pieces have not changed size. Adding the denominators would name a new, smaller unit and misrepresent the model. Subtraction removes some of the selected pieces: 7/10 − 4/10 leaves three tenths. Label a physical answer with its measurement unit.

A sum can reach or pass one whole. Eight eighths make one, while eleven eighths make one whole and three eighths. Use a strip or number line extending beyond one when needed. To check subtraction, add the removed fraction back to the remainder and rebuild the starting fraction.

explanation: A mixed number combines whole units and a fraction of another unit. In 2 3/4, the two wholes equal eight fourths, so the total is 11/4. explanation: A whole-number multiple of a fraction combines equal fractional amounts. Four groups of 2/3 are 2/3 + 2/3 + 2/3 + 2/3. Each group contains two thirds, so four groups contain eight thirds: 4 × 2/3 = 8/3. The denominator still names thirds.

Use unit-fraction structure: a/b is a copies of 1/b, so n groups contain n × a copies of 1/b. A number line shows n equal jumps of size a/b. When the product exceeds one, regroup denominator-many pieces into each whole. Eight thirds is 2 2/3.

This week multiplies a fraction by a whole number, not by another fraction. In a story, distinguish the number of groups from the amount in each group. Check the product with repeated addition or with whole and fractional parts separately. Doubling numerator and denominator would rename the fraction rather than make two groups of it.

explanation: A decimal point separates whole units from fractional place values. The first place to the right counts tenths, and the next counts hundredths. The number 0.37 means 37/100, which is also three tenths and seven hundredths. A grid of 100 equal cells can show the amount by shading 37 cells.

One tenth is ten hundredths. Splitting every tenth into ten parts gives 4/10 = 40/100, so 0.4 = 0.40. The extra zero does not make the number larger; it states the same amount using finer units. In contrast, 0.04 is only four hundredths, ten times smaller than four tenths.

A decimal can also include whole units. The number 2.06 contains two wholes, zero tenths, and six hundredths. The zero keeps the six in the hundredths place. Read the place names aloud and connect the decimal to a fraction or number-line position rather than treating the digits after the point as a separate whole number.

explanation: Tenths and hundredths are different units, so first rename them using the same part size. For 3/10 + 24/100, three tenths becomes thirty hundredths. Then 30/100 + 24/100 = 54/100. The result can also be written 0.54.

A hundred-cell grid explains the renaming. One tenth fills a row of ten cells, so each tenth contributes ten hundredths. Combining selected cells counts the total hundredths. If the sum passes one hundred cells, exchange a complete grid for a whole unit and keep the remaining cells.

This is a useful special case of unlike-denominator addition because ten and one hundred have a direct place-value relationship. Do not add denominators, and do not use this procedure as a reason to add arbitrary unlike fractions without first finding equal units. State the equivalent hundredths before combining.

explanation: Decimal comparisons use the same whole and place values. First compare the whole-number parts, then tenths, then hundredths. For 0.62 and 0.58, six tenths already exceeds five tenths; the hundredths cannot reverse that decision. A number line places the larger decimal farther right.

Rename a one-place decimal in hundredths when useful. Since 0.7 = 0.70, comparing 0.7 and 0.68 means comparing seventy and sixty-eight hundredths. More digits after the decimal point does not automatically mean more value. A trailing zero changes the name’s precision, not the quantity.

Comparing amounts also requires matching units. This week’s direct decimal comparisons use quantities measured in the same unit, with a common-sized whole. State the order using <, >, or = and justify it with place values, fraction forms, or a supplied scale.

explanation: A measurement combines a number with a unit. Changing to a smaller unit increases the number because more small units fit into the same length, mass, capacity, or time. One meter is 100 centimeters, so 3 meters is 300 centimeters. The object did not become longer; its unit changed.

Use a conversion equation to organize the groups. This lesson uses 1 km = 1,000 m, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 kg = 1,000 g, 1 L = 1,000 mL, 1 ft = 12 in, 1 yd = 3 ft, 1 hr = 60 min, and 1 min = 60 s. Stay within a single system. Mixed measurements require converting the larger unit before adding the smaller-unit part.

Label every intermediate result. Three hours and fifteen minutes is 180 minutes plus 15 minutes, not 315 minutes. Before comparing or combining measurements, express them in a common unit. An estimate should preserve the correct scale, and an inverse grouping check can confirm the conversion.

explanation: Perimeter measures the distance around a boundary and uses length units. For a rectangle, opposite sides are equal, so P = 2 × length + 2 × width. Area counts unit squares covering the interior, so A = length × width. A 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle has perimeter 20 cm but area 24 square centimeters.

Subtract the known side from that half to find the missing side. If area and one side are known, division finds how many equal rows or columns fit.

Rectangles can have the same perimeter and different areas, or the same area and different perimeters. Keep units attached so “24” does not hide which measurement is meant. For a design problem, check both constraints; satisfying the border length alone does not guarantee enough interior space.

explanation: Two rays with a shared endpoint form an angle. The endpoint is the vertex, and the rays show directions extending from it. An angle measures the turn from one ray to the other, not the lengths of drawn ray segments. A full turn has 360 equal degree units; a quarter turn has 90 degrees.

To measure with a protractor, place its center at the vertex and its zero line along one ray. Follow the scale whose zero lies on that starting ray. Where the other ray crosses that scale gives the angle measure. Protractors often show two opposite scales, so check whether the result should be smaller or larger than a right angle.

An acute angle is greater than 0 and less than 90 degrees. A right angle is 90 degrees, an obtuse angle is greater than 90 but less than 180 degrees, and a straight angle is 180 degrees. These terms describe the opening, which stays the same if the rays are extended or the drawing is rotated.

Use the described ray order and the direction of turn so you add the intended regions. Around a point the complete turn is 360 degrees. Check that all named parts cover the stated whole without gaps or overlaps. A computed angle should fit its type; a part of a right angle cannot be greater than 90 degrees.

explanation: Parallel lines stay the same distance apart and never meet in a plane; perpendicular lines meet at right angles. A segment has two endpoints, a ray has one endpoint and extends in one direction, and a line extends both ways. Use these relationships and precise angle information to classify shapes rather than relying on orientation.

A rectangle is a quadrilateral with four right angles; a square is a rectangle with four equal sides. A rhombus has four equal sides, so a square is also a rhombus. A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel opposite sides. A right triangle has one right angle, while an obtuse triangle has one obtuse angle.

A reflection symmetry line divides a shape so folding along it makes both halves coincide. Equal area alone is not enough. A nonsquare rectangle has two such lines through midpoints of opposite sides; a square has those two plus both diagonals. Count lines, not the many positions in which a shape can be rotated.

explanation: A garden design can have several different constraints: how much fence is available, how much ground must be covered, and how many plants fit in rows. Draw a labeled rectangle or state its dimensions. Perimeter governs fence length; area governs covering. A single calculation rarely answers both questions.

Choose common units before using a formula. A side of 3 m and a side of 80 cm become 300 cm and 80 cm if square centimeters are requested. To find a missing dimension, use the area product or half of the perimeter. Restrict dimensions to whole-number units only when the question says to do so.

After proposing a design, test every condition, including gates, gaps, and unused stock. A fence opening reduces fence needed but does not shrink the garden’s area. explanation: A plan often grows in stages. A display might start with six cards and add four each stage. The number at stage 5 requires four additions after the starting stage, not five. Measurement data answer a different kind of question. A line plot records the actual supplied lengths, with one mark per object. To estimate whether the objects fit a design, use every observed value and its frequency. Equivalent fractions such as 1/2 and 4/8 belong at the same measurement location.

Revise a plan when a rule, count, or exact total contradicts it. A repeated numerical pattern does not guarantee a cause, and a short list without a stated rule may permit several continuations. days: Day 1: Identify quantities, units, assumptions, and constraints.
Day 2: Choose operations and exact representations.
Day 3: Compare two feasible proposals by a stated goal.
Day 4: Revise an infeasible materials or capacity plan.
Day 5: Present a complete checked exhibition plan and explain each result.
explanation: A final plan is more than a list of answers. State the purpose of each calculation, the quantity and unit it finds, and the condition it must satisfy. A pack count must serve every participant; a material length must fit the available stock; a budget must cover the full stated price. Mark assumptions, including no cutting loss or added fees when specified.

Equivalent representations provide practical checks. A length written as 7/10 m becomes 70/100 m for a sum with hundredths. A price in dollars can become whole cents for multiplication. A quotient and remainder should rebuild the original total through divisor × quotient + remainder. These are checks on meaning as well as arithmetic.

When two proposals both work, compare them using the stated goal. Less waste, lower cost, and larger area may favor different plans. An open design can have several correct solutions, so show enough calculations for someone else to reproduce the decision. End by checking every original constraint, not merely the last calculation.
